Raw storage of a zuint vector

Source: R/types.R
zu_storage.Rd

zu_storage() returns the payload a zuint vector is stored in, and zu_from_storage() makes a zuint vector of a payload. Names are kept both ways, and no other attribute is. They are the public representation contract: a package that reads or builds zuint vectors in C, such as an Arrow or database reader, relies on these shapes and nothing else.

Usage

zu_storage(x)

zu_from_storage(payload, type)

Arguments

x

A zuint vector.

payload

A double or complex vector, as returned by zu_storage().

type

One of "int64", "uint64", "int128" or "uint128".

Value

zu_storage() returns a double or complex vector; zu_from_storage() a zuint vector of type.

Details

TypePayloadOne value
int64doublethe bits of an int64_t, as bit64's integer64
uint64doublethe bits of a uint64_t
int128complexreal part the low 64 bits, imaginary part the high 64 bits, two's complement
uint128complexreal part the low 64 bits, imaginary part the high 64 bits

The bits are in the machine's byte order, and are moved in and out of the doubles with memcpy(), never through a conversion to double, which would change NaN payloads.

Each type's NA is one bit pattern, which no value of the type has:

TypeNA bit patternAs the integer
int640x8000000000000000INT64_MIN, bit64's NA
uint640xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFUINT64_MAX
int128high word 0x8000000000000000, low word 0INT128_MIN
uint128both words 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFUINT128_MAX

So the value an engine can hold at that pattern, such as UINT64_MAX in a UBIGINT column, has no zuint form, and a reader decides what to do with it (zuarrow's lossy policy, see zuint-arrow).

These shapes and patterns change only under the rule the R API follows: with a deprecation, in a release whose NEWS.md says so. The payload is not a number: printing it or computing with it is meaningless.

Examples

p <- zu_storage(int128(-1))
p
#> [1] NaN+NaNi
zu_from_storage(p, "int128")
#> <int128[1]>
#> [1] -1
